newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: London coffee tipped to rise, Asian trade on hold.
newsitem.headline: London coffee tipped to rise, Asian trade on hold.

text.p: London robusta futures are tipped to open US$40-$160 higher later on Wednesday, while the Asian coffee business has ground to a virtual halt to wait for markets in New York and London to settle down, dealers said.

"It looks like coffee prices are on their way back up again," a coffee dealer for a commodity trading house in Singapore said. "It (London) should open $40-$100 up, but it will probably be closer to the lower level."
"Fifty higher looks more realistic although based on the values, London should go up by $140-$160," another dealer said.
The London July robusta futures contract bounced back from a recent huge sell-off and finished $40 up on the day on Tuesday at $2,150 a tonne.
Asian dealers said London will also take its cue from New York, where the July arabica futures contract climbed 10.25 cents to close on Tuesday at 264.20 U.S. cents/lb.
The bull market can easily be reignited by any news of an impending frost in Brazil or of supply problems for quality arabica beans out of Central America, dealers said.
"That will prevent aggressive selling in the market," a dealer said. "Fundamentally, supplies remain tight."
The coffee business in Asia has slowed down sharply as roasters and exporters sit on the sidelines waiting for calm to return to London and New York.
"People are looking for stability in the market. I haven't heard of anything being done in Indonesia," one dealer said.
"The roasters are not keen to buy and the things they are doing are very forward," a European trader said.
Some farmers in Indonesia have also slowed down the pace of their deliveries on expectations prices will head higher.
"If they're not greedy, they will make money," a dealer said.

Another trader added: "The Indonesian crop is coming in slow, steady and not in great volumes. Everyone is focused on what is the weather pattern in Brazil to get a clue where the market may head off next."

The price of Indonesia's Grade 4 coffee, 80 defects, was seen by the trade at around $1,870-$1,900 a tonne FOB Lampung, up slightly from yesterday's $1,865/875 a tonne on the same basis and last week's quote of $1,860/870 a tonne.
Grade 4 coffee hit a peak last week of $2,200-$2,300 a tonne on the back of the blistering rally in coffee prices.
Vietnamese coffee supplies were said to be down to the last 10,000 tonnes and no business was reported to have been done lately, dealers said.
Vietnam's Grade 2 coffee, 8.0 percent black and broken, was indicated at about $1,850-$1,900 a tonne FOB Saigon against yesterday's $1,895-$1,915 a tonne on the same basis.

Trading in the robusta coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) reached 50 lots on Tuesday. Some 16 lots of the September and November contracts finished at $1,903 and $1,900 a tonne, respectively.
Six lots of the July, January and March contracts were settled at $1,910, $1,895 and $1,890 a tonne each, SICOM said.
